name: Israel
card_headline: Israel's 27 October election left no majority, Netanyahu is caretaker while Eisenkot holds the mandate, and the Iran, Lebanon and Gaza fronts remain unsettled.
card_summary: Israel voted on 27 October and no bloc reached 61 seats: Netanyahu's camp won 53, Gadi Eisenkot's bloc 48 and Arab-led parties 19. Netanyahu stays caretaker prime minister while Eisenkot has until 6 December to build a coalition. The US-Israeli war on Iran that began on 28 February ended in an April ceasefire, but US-Iran talks are deadlocked without Israel. Israeli forces hold ground in southern Lebanon, and Israeli tanks re-entered central Gaza on 18 November.
card_local: The Times of Israel and the Jerusalem Post describe a razor-thin path: Eisenkot's 48 seats plus Shas and United Torah Judaism would reach exactly 61, while Likud presses for a unity government and Bennett's camp is reported to float a rotation. [1][2]
card_international: AP reported in June that Israel is not a party to the US-Iran deal, and Reuters reports that Israeli tanks entered central Gaza on 18 November, which some residents called the first ground raid since the 2025 ceasefire. [3][4]
card_scholar: INSS analyst Raz Zimmt (May) judges that Iran was damaged but not defeated and keeps about 440 kg of 60 percent enriched uranium, and the Israel Democracy Institute finds optimism about democratic rule down to 36 percent. [5][6]
context_md: Hamas-led militants attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages, according to AP. [7] A US-brokered Gaza ceasefire took effect in October 2025, and the last hostage's remains were recovered on 26 January 2026. [4][7] On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel attacked Iran in a campaign Israel named Operation Roaring Lion, and Hezbollah's fire brought an Israeli escalation in Lebanon. [8][9] A ceasefire with Iran began on 8 April. [10] Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on trial since 2020 for bribery, fraud and breach of trust, denies the charges. [11] Israel held its first election since the 2023 attack on 27 October 2026, with turnout of 77.9 percent. [12]

sections.title: A 53-48-19 stalemate: Eisenkot holds the mandate, Netanyahu holds the office
sections.body_md:
Israel voted on 27 October 2026, its first election since the 7 October attack, with turnout of 77.9 percent, the highest since 1999. The final count gave Likud 27 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar 21, Naftali Bennett's Together 12, the Joint List 11, the Democrats 8, Ra'am 8, Yisrael Beiteinu, United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit 7 each, and Shas and the Religious Zionist Party 6 each. By bloc that is 53 for Netanyahu's camp, 48 for the Eisenkot-led opposition and 19 for the two Arab-led parties, against 61 needed. [12]

Likud and its allies claimed, without evidence, that Arab-led parties stole the vote. The Central Elections Committee reviewed 9,069 polling stations, found no irregularities that compromised the result, and certified it on 4 November, with Justice Noam Sohlberg casting the deciding vote in its presidium. The Shin Bet separately told the committee it had intelligence of foreign funding and influence operations, while law enforcement sources told Haaretz they knew of no operation of that size. Qatar denied funding Arab-led parties. [13]

President Isaac Herzog announced on 7 November that Eisenkot would receive the mandate, after consultations in which Eisenkot drew 67 recommendations and Netanyahu 46. [1] Eisenkot has until 6 December, and Herzog can extend that by up to 14 days. [14] His bloc plus United Torah Judaism (7) and Shas (6) would reach exactly 61, though Shas publicly rejects reports that it would stand aside. [1] Talks between Likud and Yashar ended without a deal, with the premiership and Itamar Ben-Gvir's role in dispute, and Eisenkot has rejected a rotation with Netanyahu. [14] A Jerusalem Post live-blog headline on 19 November says Bennett floated a rotation deal with Netanyahu, and the page gives no detail. [2] Netanyahu remains caretaker: he cannot start a new war without a cabinet vote, but he keeps wide powers over security and foreign affairs. [15]

lenses.local: The Times of Israel reports that Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman is willing to sit with the Haredi parties and accept painful compromises on enlistment to avoid another election. [1]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera reports that Eisenkot's bloc plus the Arab-led parties would hold 67 seats, but Bennett and Liberman reject relying on them. [14]
lenses.scholar: Clingendael's July brief found the Haredi draft dominated leaders' statements before the vote, ahead of annexation and the two wars, and called the campaign wide open. [16]

sections.title: The Iran war ended in a ceasefire, not a settlement, and Israel sits outside the US-Iran talks
sections.body_md:
On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel began a joint campaign against Iran that Israel named Operation Roaring Lion. The Bank of Israel says the economy fell sharply during it, and Moody's calls it a six-week war. [8][17] Iranian and Hezbollah missiles killed 23 people in Israel as of 10 April, according to Israel's ambulance service in a Reuters factbox that Reuters did not independently verify, and Israel's Health Ministry reported 7,451 hospital admissions since the operation began. [18][19] A ceasefire began on 8 April. [10]

On 15 June the United States and Iran announced an initial deal to extend the ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. AP reported that Israel was not a party, that Defense Minister Israel Katz said Israel would strike Iran with great force if Iran attacked over Israel's Lebanon operations, and that Iran insisted any deal include an end to the Lebanon fighting. [3] Al Jazeera says that June memorandum collapsed in August and gives no reason. [20]

As of early November the strait is still closed, Iran says it will reopen it only if Washington meets seven conditions including an end to a US naval blockade, and the United States struck an Iranian anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island on 3 November, which President Trump called a minor attack. [21] Al Jazeera cites Ynet as reporting that a senior Israeli official said Israel was preparing for another round right after the US midterm elections. [20]

lenses.local: Ynet reported in February that Netanyahu's red lines were zero enrichment, removal of the roughly 450 kg stockpile, a halt to missile production and an end to proxy support, and that Israeli officials feared Washington would compromise on some of them. [22]
lenses.international: AP described Lebanon as the biggest risk to the US-Iran deal, because Iran wants the fighting there to stop. [3]
lenses.scholar: INSS's Raz Zimmt wrote in May that the war left Iran with residual capabilities and that enrichment to 90 percent could take weeks, so the neither-war-nor-peace situation is unstable and unlikely to last. [5]

sections.title: Israel holds ground in southern Lebanon, Syria talks are frozen, and the Houthis threaten the Red Sea
sections.body_md:
Hezbollah fired at Israel after the 28 February attack on Iran, and Israel escalated across Lebanon. Lebanon's health ministry counts 8,920 people killed and 30,559 injured by Israeli strikes between 8 October 2023 and 1 September 2026, and L'Orient-Le Jour says Israel occupies more than 600 square kilometres of Lebanese territory. A new ceasefire followed the US-Iran memorandum in June, yet Israel still carries out daily operations in the south. [9] The newsru.co.il report for 19 November lists strikes in the Bekaa and near Nabatieh, a demolition in the south, and an IDF buffer zone. [23] Katz said in June that Israel would stay in Lebanon indefinitely. [3]

Under a US-brokered trilateral framework, Israel is to withdraw from demarcated pilot zones and Hezbollah is to disarm. Lebanon's presidency accuses Israel of failing to comply. The UN force UNIFIL, present since 1978, has a mandate that expires in December, Washington opposes renewal, and Mike Waltz visited Beirut this month to discuss an alternative. Lebanon wants a multinational ground force, which Israel has rejected. [24]

In Syria, Israel and Damascus agreed on paper around the start of the year to nearly everything, including security zones in the south, according to Reuters via Al-Monitor. Talks were suspended after the Iran war began, and they met in Jordan on 23 August, with no final agreement reported. Syria wants Israel back at its pre-8 December 2024 positions. [25] The Houthis, who nominally joined the Iran war in March, announced a missile barrage on Israel and a ban on Israeli shipping in the Red Sea on 8 June, a route carrying about 12 percent of global maritime trade. [10]

lenses.local: L'Orient-Le Jour, a Lebanese outlet, reports that Israeli operations in the south continue despite the June ceasefire. [9]
lenses.international: The National's Nada Homsi reports Western diplomats warning of a security and humanitarian vacuum if UNIFIL leaves. [24]

sections.title: Gaza and the West Bank from the Israeli side: a ceasefire with soldiers dead and a new ground push
sections.body_md:
The Gaza ceasefire has held on paper since October 2025, but the fighting has not stopped. On 18 November Israeli tanks advanced into central Gaza west of the Yellow Line, which marks the area Israel controls. The Israeli military said it was acting against Hamas infrastructure, and Hamas called the raid a dangerous escalation and a ceasefire violation. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire, and the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have died. Israel says Hamas is regrouping and rearming, and Hamas says Israel is trying to derail the deal. A Board of Peace report to the UN Security Council accuses both sides of missing their commitments and warns the ceasefire could collapse. [4]

All living hostages came home, and the remains of the last, police officer Ran Gvili, were recovered on 26 January. The plan's second phase, with an international security force, Hamas disarmament, an Israeli pullback and reconstruction, is still unfinished. [7]

In the West Bank, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks from 1 to 26 October, the most in any month since it began counting in 2006. Israel began a large operation in Hebron on 23 October, the day two Palestinians who attacked an Israeli checkpoint were killed, and Hebron's municipality says about 3,000 people were displaced, a figure OCHA is still verifying. [26] The Palestinian Territories page on this site covers casualty counts and aid access in detail.

lenses.local: Newsru.co.il reports that the IDF holds a buffer zone covering more than 60 percent of Gaza and answers alleged violations with strikes, a single-outlet claim. [23]
lenses.international: Reuters reports that Israel says Hamas is rearming while Hamas accuses Israel of trying to derail the deal. [4]

sections.title: The cabinet voted to defy the Supreme Court, and Netanyahu's pardon request sits with Herzog
sections.body_md:
On Sunday 5 July the cabinet voted unanimously to reject a Supreme Court order of 17 June that the media regulatory council keep functioning, saying it would act through all legal means to nullify the decision. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said the decision undermines the rule of law, and President Herzog called defiance a red line. Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi called the vote a historic step to return the state to the people. [27] Moody's cited the cabinet's vote when it flagged weakening judicial independence as a risk to Israel's rating. [17]

Netanyahu is Israel's first sitting prime minister charged with a crime. He denies the bribery, fraud and breach of trust charges, and his trial began in 2020. He asked Herzog for a pardon on 30 November 2025 after Donald Trump urged one, and there is no precedent for a mid-trial pardon. [28][11] On 26 April Herzog said he would consider the request only after efforts to reach a plea agreement outside the courtroom were exhausted. [11] Netanyahu's testimony, set to resume on 27 April after a pause of more than two months, was canceled at the last minute, and Hebrew media reported that his lawyer cited security concerns. He has testified 80 times. [29]

On accountability for 7 October, the Knesset Constitution Committee advanced a bill in June for a commission with six members, three chosen by the coalition and three by the opposition, that can start work with three. The opposition says it will boycott and wants a state commission, and the High Court had given the government until 1 July to propose a framework. [30] Reporters Without Borders ranks Israel 116th of 180 in its 2026 index, down from 112th, and notes that only journalists embedded with the IDF may enter Gaza. [31]

lenses.local: Haaretz's editorial, as relayed by The National, said the cabinet had effectively ended the rule of law; this draft did not read Haaretz directly. [27]
lenses.international: Reuters reports that Herzog wants a plea deal first and that Trump has repeatedly urged a pardon. [11]
lenses.scholar: The Israel Democracy Institute's August survey found 59 percent of Israelis saw a high likelihood of election interference by Israeli political entities, and 56 percent thought the losing side might refuse to accept the results. [6]

sections.title: At home: 2,100 Haredi enlistees from 79,000 orders, and 252 Arab citizens killed in 2025
sections.body_md:
The Haredi draft is the issue that splits Netanyahu's own bloc. On 26 April the High Court unanimously ordered the government to condition five welfare benefits on enlistment and to take criminal proceedings against evaders, and it called the police's refusal to arrest them an unacceptable mass violation of law. More than 79,000 conscription orders have gone to Haredi men since the court's 2024 ruling, about 2,100 have enlisted, and police proactively arrested 17 men between January 2025 and January 2026. [32] Clingendael found the draft made up 30 percent of leaders' statements, ahead of annexation at 23 percent and the Iran and Hezbollah wars at 19 percent each, and notes that Shas and United Torah Judaism oppose any conscription law. [16] Liberman says a draft law must pass the IDF chief, the High Court and the rabbis. [2]

Violence inside the Arab community is a separate emergency. The Abraham Initiatives counts 252 Arab citizens killed in 2025, the highest year on record, and more than 140 by early July 2026, 12 percent above the same point in 2025. Israeli police say they treat every incident with the utmost seriousness and cite joint task forces. [33] For Arab respondents in the Israel Democracy Institute's survey, a party's position on crime in Arab society was the top voting issue, at 53.5 percent. [6] Arab-led parties won 19 seats on 27 October. [12]

lenses.local: The Times of Israel's Jeremy Sharon documents how few Haredi men have enlisted despite 79,000 orders. [32]
lenses.international: AFP, carried by Al-Monitor, reports that 2026 would exceed the 2025 total if the current rate continues. [33]
lenses.scholar: The Israel Democracy Institute finds that about two-thirds of Jewish respondents and one-third of Arab respondents call 7 October a central factor in their vote. [6]

sections.title: The economy rebounded after the Iran war, with a deficit near 4.4 to 5.3 percent of GDP and a Baa1 rating
sections.body_md:
The economy shrank in the first quarter, when the Iran war began, and recovered quickly in the second, according to the Bank of Israel. Its research department forecasts growth of 5.6 percent in 2026 and 7.5 percent in 2027, or 3.4 and 5.1 percent excluding production abroad by Israeli companies. The Monetary Committee held its rate at 3.25 percent on 21 October, with inflation at 1.6 percent in the twelve months to September, and the shekel had weakened 3.1 percent against the dollar through 20 October. [8] The IMF's staff project 3.5 percent growth in 2026, down from 4.8 percent before the war. [34]

The deficit is the main strain. The Bank of Israel expects 4.4 percent of GDP in 2026 if defense spending gets no more money, while the IMF's baseline is a central government deficit of 5.3 percent against a budget ceiling of 4.9 percent. General government debt was 68 percent of GDP at the end of 2025. The IMF rates the likelihood of geopolitical escalation as high and models a downside case with defense spending at 9 percent of GDP. [8][34] Moody's kept Israel at Baa1 with a stable outlook in July, cut its 2026 growth forecast to 3.7 percent and called the ceasefires with Iran, Hezbollah and Hamas fragile. [17] The Bank of Israel says Israel's credit-default-swap premium stayed close to its prewar level. [8]

lenses.local: The Bank of Israel assumes fighting stays at low intensity and says geopolitical developments will significantly influence inflation, activity and the exchange rate. [8]
lenses.international: Moody's says an upgrade is possible if ceasefires hold and public finances improve, and a new escalation with lasting damage could lead to a downgrade. [17]
lenses.scholar: IMF staff recommend cutting the central government deficit to about 2.5 percent of GDP over three years, with revenue measures first. [34]

sections.title: Abroad: 60 percent of Americans view Israel unfavorably, and the EU stays split on its trade agreement
sections.body_md:
Pew's March 2026 survey of 3,507 US adults found 60 percent had an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 53 percent in 2025 and 42 percent in 2022, and 59 percent had little or no confidence in Netanyahu on world affairs. Republicans remain favorable on balance, at 58 percent, while about 8 in 10 Democrats are unfavorable. [35] INSS lists the erosion of Israel's standing in the United States among the dilemmas the Iran war left behind. [5] Israelis notice: half of respondents in the Israel Democracy Institute's survey said relations with the United States matter to their vote. [6]

In Europe, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia pushed on 21 April to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement, and France and Sweden proposed tariffs on goods from Israeli settlements. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said support was insufficient for full or partial suspension, and Germany and Italy were not expected to back such measures. A full suspension needs all 27 member states. [36]

lenses.local: Israel Democracy Institute respondents rate relations with the United States as a voting factor for half of those surveyed. [6]
lenses.international: Euronews reports that Kallas said there was no change in member states' positions on suspending the agreement. [36]
lenses.scholar: Pew finds majorities of adults under 50 in both US parties rate Israel and Netanyahu negatively. [35]

podcasts.why: Covers who might win, small parties, Trump's influence and how the vote could affect the Gaza and Iran wars. The page lists Sachs under two affiliations.

podcasts.guest: Daniel Levy, US Middle East Project
podcasts.why: Asks how a coalition's makeup would shape policy on the West Bank, Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and Syria. The outlet is Abu Dhabi-based.

media.title: NAZA
media.creator: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor
media.where: Won the special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival in September 2026; this link is a Times of Israel opinion piece, and the page does not give a public release date.
media.why: The film alleges that the IDF approved Gaza strikes knowing large numbers of civilians would die, and the IDF strongly denies this. Israeli officials, including IDF chief Eyal Zamir, condemned it, and it became a campaign issue.

factchecks.claim: Arab-led parties stole the 27 October election.
factchecks.evidence: The Central Elections Committee reviewed 9,069 polling stations, examined every complaint and found no irregularities that compromised the vote or changed the outcome, then certified the results on 4 November. The Shin Bet separately told the committee of foreign funding and influence operations, but law enforcement sources told Haaretz they knew of no operation of that size, and Qatar denied funding Arab-led parties. Investigations continue, and the committee chair said they would not materially alter the result.

sources.title: Israel vote results confirmed as election commission rejects fraud claims

factchecks.claim: US and Israeli strikes destroyed Iran's nuclear programme.
factchecks.by: President Trump, who said it was obliterated after the June 2025 strikes, per Reuters
factchecks.evidence: A preliminary US Defense Intelligence Agency assessment reported by Reuters said the June 2025 strikes set Iran's programme back only a few months, and the White House called that report flat out wrong. The administration later told the UN Security Council the programme had been degraded. After the 2026 war, INSS estimates Iran still holds about 440 kg of 60 percent enriched uranium, and enrichment to 90 percent could take weeks if done clandestinely.

sources.title: US airstrikes failed to destroy Iran's nuclear sites, sources say
In the Wake of Roaring Lion: Preliminary Insights, Hypotheses, and Dilemmas for Israel

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters and AFP file from Israel almost daily, and several English-language Israeli outlets cover politics and security in real time. [4][1][2] Think tanks such as INSS, the Israel Democracy Institute and Clingendael publish steady analysis. [5][6][16] The gap is Hebrew and Arabic sourcing, which this draft reads only through English editions. [32]

severity.basis: Israel fought a six-week war with Iran, still operates daily in southern Lebanon, and sent tanks into central Gaza on 18 November. [17][9][4] Iranian and Hezbollah missiles killed 23 people in Israel as of 10 April, and 252 Arab citizens were killed in crime-related violence in 2025. [18][33]
Israel's health system admitted 7,451 people during the Iran war, but Israel's own population faces limited displacement and hunger, and the Bank of Israel reports a quick recovery. [19][8]

The cabinet voted to reject a Supreme Court ruling, the attorney general said it undermines the rule of law, and RSF ranks Israel 116th of 180. [27][31] Elections were held with 77.9 percent turnout and certified despite Likud fraud claims. [12][13]
Moody's holds Baa1 with a stable outlook and the Bank of Israel forecasts 5.6 percent growth, but the IMF projects a 5.3 percent central government deficit against a 4.9 percent ceiling. [17][8][34]
The hostages are home and the Gaza ceasefire survives, but a war with Iran, a Lebanon occupation, a court-defiance vote and a stalemated election all came within twelve months. [7][4][27][12]

parts.basis: The United States fought alongside Israel against Iran, runs the Gaza and Lebanon diplomacy, and negotiates with Iran without Israel at the table. [3][24][20]
The Houthi shipping ban threatens the Red Sea route that carries about 12 percent of global maritime trade, and Israel's own economy is small and recovering. [10][8]
The Iran war drew in Hezbollah and the Houthis, and Iran says any new attack would bring a response without geographical limits. [10][20]
Israeli strikes killed 8,920 people in Lebanon over the period to September 2026, and the Iran war produced casualties in Iran, Israel, Lebanon and Gulf states. [9][18]
Katz says Israel will stay in land it holds in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, and EU states are split over suspending the Association Agreement. [3][36]

summary: Israel scores high because its wars involve the United States directly and reach Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza at once. [3][10] The economic score stays moderate because Israel's own weight in trade is limited, though shipping routes near it matter. [10]
gi.up: A resumed US or Israeli attack on Iran, a collapse of the Gaza ceasefire, or a closure of the Red Sea route would raise it.
gi.down: A signed US-Iran settlement that holds, a Lebanon withdrawal under the trilateral framework and a durable Gaza second phase would lower it.

gaps: Hebrew and Arabic-language Israeli press was read only through English editions (Times of Israel, Jerusalem Post, Ynet, JNS); Haaretz, Maariv, Kan and Israel Hayom were not opened directly, and the Haaretz material here is relayed by Al Jazeera and The National. Local sourcing for Arab-Israeli voices is thin.
No Israeli government primary documents (prime minister's office, Knesset records, IDF statements) were read. Positions come through Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera and the Israeli outlets listed.

Al Jazeera and The National are flagged as state-linked and supply many items; wires, Israeli outlets and think tanks balance them, but several facts (the August collapse of the June US-Iran memorandum, the 22 November end of Likud-Yashar talks, the Shin Bet foreign-funding claim) rest on one outlet.

The latest coalition development (the 22 November end of Likud-Yashar talks) was read only in Al Jazeera's update to a 15 November article; the linked report was not opened. Nothing after 23 November was confirmed.

Casualty counts come from different bodies and dates and were not reconciled: 23 killed in Israel by Iranian and Lebanese missiles (as of 10 April, unverified), an unattributed 42 in a headline, 7,451 hospital admissions, Lebanon's 8,920, and Gaza's counts, which the Palestinian Territories page covers.
The Iran war's full toll, the June US-Iran memorandum's terms and why it collapsed were not established; the 2026 Iran war is described from Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera, the Bank of Israel and INSS only.

Not covered: ICC and ICJ proceedings, Israeli arms and aid arrangements with the United States, Hezbollah's current strength, Gaza hospitals, East Jerusalem, detainees, October 7 hostages' families, antisemitism abroad and Israeli emigration. Houthi activity after June was not checked.

Podcast and documentary entries point to episode and opinion pages, not streaming pages, and lengths are not shown. Book years come from publisher and review pages and one is inferred from a review date.
Whether the Knesset passed the October 7 inquiry bill, and the Supreme Court's later treatment of the media-council order, were not checked.
